title: Bill sales give the Bank a short-term instrument for absorbing funds
summary: The April 27 rules govern sales of bills issued and accepted by the Bank itself. A buyer exchanges funds for a central-bank claim until the bill matures. The three-month limit runs from the day after the sale. Eligible counterparties are selected from specified groups including financial institutions, domestic and foreign securities firms, securities finance firms and money-market dealers. The rules locate the operation at the head office.

The Bank would sell the bills at a discount through competitive bidding and determine each operation’s timing, amount and participants in light of market conditions. These are operating powers effective on April 27. They do not order a particular sale or report how much liquidity was absorbed. For research purposes the effect on funds outstanding depends on settlement of new bills and repayments as existing bills mature.

questions.question: When did bill sales actually withdraw funds?
questions.detail: Use issue-level settlement and redemption records to reconstruct net cash flows by day. An announcement of terms, the award date and the settlement date can all differ.

questions.question: How were Bank bills priced relative to other short government-sector claims?
questions.detail: Match maturity, settlement conventions and secondary-market liquidity. Compare auction discount rates with like-dated instruments without treating every spread as a premium for default risk.

questions.question: Did auction participation concentrate absorption at a handful of firms?
questions.detail: Where awards by participant are available, compare amounts and bidding rates across eligible groups. Eligibility by category does not show who bid or how concentrated awards were.
